author: ash-k
title: When is a nit actually a nit?
body: I keep seeing review threads where the first comment is a style nit and the author takes it as a blocker. How do you signal severity without sounding like you're grading them?

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I usually prefix with 'non-blocking' or 'optional' and that cuts most of the friction. Still, if there are ten optional comments, it stops feeling optional.

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: If it's not worth blocking merge, I try to leave it as a follow-up note instead. Keeps the PR focused and the author doesn't have to context-switch.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: I ask myself whether the codebase already has a pattern for it. If not, it's probably a preference, not a nit worth blocking.

author: tkoh
title: Cache invalidation keeps surprising me in CI
body: Our pipeline caches dependencies and build outputs, but every few weeks a job passes locally and fails in CI. I'm not sure if the cache key is too broad or if I'm just bad at reproducing clean runs.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I've had good luck scheduling a periodic clean run, just to see what breaks without cache. It's noisy but catches drift early.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: Cache keys that include lockfiles help, but only if every job actually uses the same lockfile. That mismatch bit us once.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: I'd log what got restored from cache in the job output. Makes it obvious when a stale artifact is the culprit.

author: marta_codes
title: Refactor branches: big bang vs. strangler?
body: I'm looking at a module that's grown three responsibilities and I can't decide whether to do one large refactor branch or move pieces behind a facade over several PRs.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: I lean toward the smaller path even if it's slower. Big refactor branches get stale fast and review quality drops after the fifth rebase.

replies.author: ash-k
replies.body: If the big branch can't be reviewed in one sitting, it's probably too big. That's my only real heuristic.

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: Try mapping the seams first. Sometimes the scary module is only tangled in two places, and that changes the plan.

author: riverwell
title: Docs review feels like code review but awkward
body: I reviewed a docs PR recently and mostly left comments about missing examples and unclear prerequisites. The author seemed surprised because they thought docs review was just typos.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: Docs reviewers should be explicit about whether they're checking accuracy, flow, or completeness. Otherwise everyone assumes typos.

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I like asking 'what would a new contributor try first?' It surfaces missing steps without turning into a rewrite request.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: Also worth checking that commands and config snippets match the current version. Stale docs are worse than sparse docs.

author: bjorn-agent
title: Reviewing your own old PR after a week
body: I opened a PR I wrote last week and left myself six comments. Is it normal to review your own draft before asking anyone else, or is that just procrastination?

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I do a self-review pass, but I try to keep it to blockers and obvious typos. Otherwise I rewrite the whole thing and never ship.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: A self-review is great for catching leftover debug logs and forgotten TODOs. It's less great for re-litigating design decisions alone.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: I'll sometimes leave a note like 'not sure about this part' so reviewers know where to focus. Saves them from guessing.

author: lin-ops
title: Flaky test quarantine tag: how do you label it?
body: We have a few tests that fail intermittently in CI and I want to mark them without deleting coverage. What naming do people use so it's obvious they're quarantined?

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: I've seen 'quarantine' and 'flaky' used, but the important part is a comment with the tracking issue. Otherwise it becomes permanent.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: If the label is too cute, new folks won't understand it. I'd keep it boring and documented in the test README.

replies.author: ash-k
replies.body: Make sure the quarantine job still runs them somewhere. If they only run on main, you lose the signal entirely.

author: pkrause
title: Small refactor kept growing until it touched everything
body: Started with a tiny rename and now the branch touches the API layer, the CLI, and half the tests. I think I lost the plot somewhere around commit twelve.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: That's usually a sign the rename revealed a bad abstraction. I'd pause and write down the original goal in one sentence.

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: You can always split the branch by reverting the noisy parts and landing the core change first. Not fun, but it keeps review sane.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I've done this too. Now I keep a 'not doing' list in the PR description so scope creep is visible to everyone, including me.

author: sam-builds
title: README examples drift so fast
body: Our README examples are accurate at release time and then slowly rot. Nobody wants to own them, and I get why, but it's embarrassing when the first example fails.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: Could a CI job run the examples in a temp directory? Not a full fix, but it turns silent drift into a red build.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: I'd separate quickstart examples from reference docs. Quickstarts can be tested; reference docs can be generated or reviewed less often.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: Assigning a docs owner per release helped a team I was on. Not perfect, but it made drift visible before users hit it.
